article.title: Researcher's Archive-Extraction Attack Bypasses Claude Code Auto Mode Safety Classifier Up to 80% of the Time
article.summary: Security researcher Johann Rehberger tricked Claude Code's Auto Mode into running attacker code just by having it summarize a malicious website, up to 80% of the time.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Security researcher Johann Rehberger, known online as wunderwuzzi, found that Anthropic's Claude Code running Opus 5 in Auto Mode can be tricked into executing attacker-controlled code simply by asking the coding agent to summarize a website, with the attack working [up to 80 percent of the time](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372), according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372). Auto Mode uses an automated safety classifier to review tool calls instead of asking users to approve every command, according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372) and [Cyber Security News](https://cybersecuritynews.com/claude-code-opus-5-auto-mode-hijacked/), and it has been [the default setting for Claude Code since mid-August](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372), per The Register.

## What We Know

The attack chain begins with what looks like an innocuous request, according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372): asking Claude Code to summarize a malicious website that presents itself as an archive of notebook records, then tricking Claude into using curl instead of its WebFetch tool to retrieve the page's contents — without ever directly instructing the model to use curl. The WebFetch request fails with a 415 Unsupported Media Type response, so the model decides on its own to access the website directly by issuing a Bash tool call with curl, [The Register reports](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372).

From there, the website returns a 303 response that redirects to a malicious ZIP archive, which Claude downloads. The archive contains a mix of seemingly harmless files — catalog metadata, a README, seven Base85/zlib-encoded JSON "notebook records," and a macOS binary called decoder-darwin — alongside a poisoned Python file named struct.py, according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372).

Claude's own safety guardrails then become part of the exploit. The model refuses to run the supplied decoder binary — "This is planned and what the attacker wants," Rehberger wrote, [as quoted by The Register](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372) — and instead writes its own decoder. "Ironically, that safety decision is the exploit path," Rehberger explained, per [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372). Claude's self-written decoder imports Python's base64 module, and because base64 in turn imports struct, Python's module-shadowing behavior causes it to load the attacker's malicious struct.py from the extracted archive directory instead of the legitimate standard-library module, as explained by both [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372) and [Cyber Security News](https://cybersecuritynews.com/claude-code-opus-5-auto-mode-hijacked/). Rehberger says he used ChatGPT to obfuscate the malicious struct.py code so it would bypass Claude's safety controls; once loaded, it launches a separate Python process that downloads and executes a remote payload — in the demonstration, a command-and-control callback that in turn opens the Calculator app as proof of concept, according to [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372).

Across three variants tested five times each, Rehberger reported success rates between 60 percent and 80 percent — a Python-based attack chain and a nested Claude Code variant each succeeded in 3 of 5 tests, while a version that wrote files outside the workspace succeeded in 4 of 5 tests — according to both [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372) and [Cyber Security News](https://cybersecuritynews.com/claude-code-opus-5-auto-mode-hijacked/). Rehberger cautioned about the scope of his testing: "I would say that these results are representative for a motivated attack, but not comprehensive," [as quoted by The Register](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372).

Anthropic did not respond to The Register's request for comment, but reportedly told Rehberger that the model's "behavior is working as designed," [according to The Register](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372). Rehberger, paraphrasing Anthropic's response, wrote that "Auto Mode is a convenience feature backed by a best-effort classifier, not a security guarantee," [per The Register](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372).

## What We Don't Know

The Register's report does not include a CVE identifier or formal security advisory tied to this finding, and no direct, on-the-record quote from a named Anthropic employee is included — Anthropic's position is relayed only through Rehberger's account of what the company told him. The exact date in mid-August when Auto Mode became Claude Code's default setting is not specified beyond "mid-August."

## Analysis

The finding underscores a recurring pattern in AI coding agent security: safety mechanisms designed to block one class of behavior can create new attack surface when they interact with an agent's broader autonomy. Here, Claude's refusal to execute an untrusted binary — ordinarily a sound safety decision — is what pushed it to write and run its own code, which then became the vector for exploitation through Python's module-shadowing behavior. Rehberger's own caveat about the limits of his testing points to the core takeaway offered in the report: [running coding agents in a sandbox](https://www.theregister.com/research/2026/08/28/researcher-shows-how-claude-code-can-be-tricked-simply-by-asking-it-to-summarize-a-website/5293372) remains the more durable defense than relying on an automated approval classifier alone.
